rv.q: The production's greatest strength is its star-crossed lovers, Orlando Bloom and Condola Rashad, who bring genuine chemistry and emotional depth to their iconic roles.
But the tragic events that follow pass in such an anticlimactic blur that when our hero and heroine finally off themselves, it’s hard to feel bereft.
Credit David Leveaux with trying to make Shakespeare cool, even if this uneven production sometimes misses the mark by falling in love with its visual effects.
The tragedy also survives its gimmicky update to modern-ish times.
But the dreamy intoxication that such a heady fragrance might transmit is largely missing from David Leveaux's snoozy modern-dress production, along with poetry and heat.
Chemistry is what you look for in the title pairing, and that’s noticeably lacking here.
It's gorgeously ambient, like some plush hotel lobby where the famous and almost-famous mingle agreeably among the water features and fire pits.

Alas, these lovers are not just star-crossed but so mismatched that they could be from different galaxies in director David Leveaux's busy-with-brainstorms but broad and surprisingly unmoving production.
In this, his Broadway and Shakespeare debuts, the British actor is handsome but lacks stage presence.
It's just another missed opportunity in this dutiful but rather dull production.

Though there are moments when the tragic duo's chemistry falters and things cool down, you're advised to take a fashion cue from Brent Carver's linen-clad, yogi-like Friar Laurence should you attend: wear breathable fibers, and just to be safe, bring a fan.
It is fine to transplant Shakespeare's play to modern times, but if Leveaux has a compelling concept it doesn't come across.
Despite some nice touches in this uneven production, the star-crossed lovers were doomed long before that first kiss.

It's the most sensually stirring scene in this Romeo, which for all its style and bluster fails to produce a compelling connection between its stars or with the audience.
Bloom, after making a bafflingly cheesy entrance on a motorcycle, gives an empty, uninteresting performance marked by shrill line readings.
In this case, it's hard to find a reason for restaging "Romeo and Juliet" – and, as it turns out, lots of reasons not to.

Regrettably, it's the stage-long row of flames that rises from the floor and makes the occasional dramatic cameo that provides any kind of heat in director David Leveaux's soggy production of Romeo and Juliet.
But anyone expecting to perceive more than a glimmer of Shakespeare’s sumptuous canvas should stay away.
But these gimmicky touches can’t substitute for the missing ardor of the title lovers or the flatness of the staging.
